sittings.why_these_chairs: Plato speaks first because the Republic asks this question about its own guardians and answers that they must be formed so as not to need another guardian. Madison, named by the report for Federalist 51, built the American answer: power checked by rival power. Locke, named for consent, wrote that the people themselves are judge of whether their trustees keep the trust. Blackstone set down the common-law rule that elections must be free and undue influence on electors is illegal, which speaks to the deception charge. Machiavelli, in the Discourses, argued that a republic needs a power to accuse and also warned against calumny, the two edges of a pre-election probe. Juvenal, named for the line usually rendered as who will guard the guards themselves, is left off: the line comes from a satire on marriage, not politics, and no verified public-domain translation was fetched tonight. Peltola, both Dan Sullivans, Gov. Dunleavy, DOJ officials and the DSCC are context only.

opening.text: Tonight's subject: who guards the guardians, and how does a free people protect elections from deception without handing that protection to the very power that stands to gain from it? The report gives one side, framed as election integrity, as saying that if a party engineered a name-alike candidate to trick voters, that is fraud on the franchise, and the state should investigate before results are certified. The other side, framed as executive overreach, says that using federal grand juries and a pre-emptive suit to hold up certification days before a vote looks like the government putting a thumb on the scale, especially with no evidence anyone actually voted by mistake. We take no view on who did what in Alaska; no one has been charged. Plato, you begin.

turn.text: The question your report asks is the one my Socrates turned over when he described the guardians of the city. His answer was almost a joke: “that a guardian should require another guardian to take care of him is ridiculous indeed.” (Republic III, 403e) He meant that the only lasting safeguard is the character of those who hold power. A guardian who needs watching has already failed, and adding a second watcher only moves the problem up one level.

turn.text: So I would tell the defenders that they are right about history: Christian faith did more than any other force to shape American habits of liberty. And I would tell them, too, that the source of that power was its distance from government. sittings.why_these_chairs: Augustine speaks first because he wrote, in his letter to Deogratias, on whether those outside the visible people of God could share in Christ's salvation, holding both that salvation is through this religion alone and that it reached some in other nations. Aquinas wrote on implicit faith in Christ among those without explicit revelation. Pascal wrote that God is known only through Jesus Christ as mediator, the sharpest statement of the critics' premise. Karl Rahner, named for the anonymous Christian, closes; he is in copyright and paraphrased only. Elijah on Carmel, the council of Acts 15 and Jesus' words in John are set by the moderator from the text. Advocates of insider movement missiology, named by the report, are left off because their writing is recent and in copyright. Judah Smith, his friend and his critics are context only.

opening.text: Tonight's subject: exclusivity and conversion, what it means to belong to Christ, and whether identity follows faith or faith follows identity. The report gives one side, the critics, as saying that Jesus' claim is exclusive: “I am the way, the truth, and the life: no man cometh unto the Father, but by me.” (John 14:6) Following him means leaving other gods, not adding him to a pantheon; Elijah's challenge is the old form of it: “How long halt ye between two opinions? if the LORD be God, follow him: but if Baal, then follow him.” (1 Kings 18:21) The other side, Smith's defenders, says he was describing a real person's journey, that labels and church culture can block people from Jesus, and that growth in faith takes time; they can point to the apostles' decision at Jerusalem: “Wherefore my sentence is, that we trouble not them, which from among the Gentiles are turned to God” (Acts 15:19) We take no view on the pastor or his friend. Augustine, you begin.

turn.text: A pagan critic asked me why, if Christ is the only way, he came so late, and what became of those who lived before. I answered that Christ was preached from the beginning in many ways, and that some outside Israel belonged to him. Yet I held the exclusive claim firmly: “Thus the salvation provided by this religion, by which alone, as alone true, true salvation is truly promised, was never wanting to any one who was worthy of it, and he to whom it was wanting was not worthy of it.” (Letter 102 (to Deogratias), §15)

turn.text: The defenders may take comfort here: God works in people before they can name everything he is doing. But my distinction is exact and the critics should press it. Implicit faith belonged, for me, to those who had not received the revelation, not to those who have heard it and choose to hold Christ alongside other gods. Once someone knows Jesus, the journey must move toward explicit faith in him, and that includes leaving what contradicts it.

sittings.why_these_chairs: Vincent of Lérins speaks first because his Commonitory sets the classic test for what belongs to the Church's faith and how it may develop. Pius XII wrote Mediator Dei, which treats lex orandi, lex credendi, reserves the liturgy to Church authority, and commends private devotions; it is in copyright and paraphrased only. Ignatius of Antioch wrote the earliest rule tying the Church's worship to the bishop. Newman wrote on how doctrine develops without being altered. The lost-sheep parable, named by the report, is set by the moderator. Fr. James Martin, Outreach and the Catholic Herald are context only.

turn.text: I proposed a test for what belongs to the Church's faith: “in the Catholic Church itself, all possible care must be taken, that we hold that faith which has been believed everywhere, always, by all” (The Commonitory, ch. 2, §6) The Confiteor, with its appeal to Mary, the angels and the saints, has been prayed in that way for many centuries. The critics stand on my ground: a prayer so long received is not any one writer's to revise.

turn.text: But I was not an enemy of growth. I asked whether there is progress in the Church and answered yes, much, “Yet on condition that it be real progress, not alteration of the faith.” (The Commonitory, ch. 23, §54) A private devotion that adds prayers for a group may be growth. A text that replaces the Mother of God and the saints with figures of its own choosing alters what the prayer asks for, and so what it teaches.

In a higher world it is otherwise, but here below to live is to change, and to be perfect is to have changed often.” (Development of Christian Doctrine, ch. I, sect. I, §7) The Church has long adapted its devotions to new peoples and needs, and the supporters are right that reaching those who feel far away is one of its oldest instincts.

turn.text: But my first note of a true development was preservation of type: it keeps the same idea and does not reverse what came before (Development of Christian Doctrine, ch. V, paraphrased). The communion of saints is part of the type. A development would bring the marginalized into that communion; putting chosen ancestors in place of Mary and the saints changes the type.

chairs.modern_read: Newman taught that the Church changes in order to stay the same, which supports pastoral adaptation. But he required that real developments preserve the original character, and replacing Mary and the saints would change it rather than develop it.
